summary: Provides information and requirements for how IP addresses should be handled by WebRTC implementations.

eli5.summary: Rules for how a browser shares its network address during a call.

subtitle: Four modes that trade media quality against how many of a user's IP addresses a web page can see.

tldr.problem: To set up a peer-to-peer call, WebRTC gathers many IP addresses and hands them to the web application, which can reveal more about the user than ordinary HTTP does, such as a VPN user's real ISP address or a private LAN address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four modes, from enumerating all addresses to forcing all media through a proxy, and recommends Mode 1 only with user consent and Mode 2 otherwise.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get a framework for balancing performance and privacy, with defaults that still allow direct peer-to-peer connections without exposing more than needed.

today: RFC 8828 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Why IP Addresses Need Handling Rules
sections.content:
One of WebRTC's key features is its support of peer-to-peer connections. Setting one up involves connection attempts from various IP addresses. As a result, WebRTC may allow a web application to learn more about the user than an application that only uses HTTP.

The RFC summarizes the concerns and recommends how implementations should handle the trade-off between privacy and media performance. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in BCP 14 (RFC 2119 and RFC 8174).
sections.eli5: Making a call directly between two computers means sharing some addresses. Sharing too many can tell a website more about you than you want.

sections.title: The Problem: What Gets Revealed
sections.content:
WebRTC uses Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE, RFC 8445) to find several local and remote addresses and test each pair. It collects them with STUN and TURN. These addresses are passed to the web application so it can send them to the remote side, so the application learns more than the single public address an HTTP server would see.

The extra information falls into three categories:

  • A multihomed client can expose extra public addresses. With a split-tunnel VPN, WebRTC can discover both the VPN's public address and the ISP public address underneath it.
  • A client behind a NAT can expose its private addresses, often RFC 1918 addresses.
  • A client behind a classical application proxy, where direct Internet access is still permitted, has its public address revealed because STUN checks bypass the proxy.

The RFC calls the first concern the most significant, because some users run a VPN for anonymity. Others, such as corporate VPN users, may prefer that media goes directly rather than through the VPN.

Private IPv4 addresses are the second concern. Some carry little entropy (192.168.0.2 is a fairly common address), but in the worst case they can carry 24 bits of entropy with an indefinite lifetime, which makes a fingerprinting surface. They can also let pages in isolated browsing contexts, such as normal and private browsing, discover they run on the same device. The third concern is the least common, since proxy administrators can already control it with firewall policy.
sections.eli5: A website could learn which VPN you are hiding behind, the secret room numbers inside your home network, or the address your proxy was supposed to hide. Each of these is a different kind of leak.

sections.title: Goals and Principles
sections.content:
Blunt solutions that disable WebRTC or make it much harder to use are undesirable, because peer-to-peer support can have privacy benefits of its own. The RFC sets three goals: a framework for understanding the problem, settings that each strike a different balance between performance and privacy, and recommended defaults that perform reasonably without exposing addresses against user expectations.

Four principles shape the design:

  • By default WebRTC traffic follows typical IP routing, so only the system's typical public addresses (or an enterprise TURN server's) are visible. It should still be possible to use all interfaces for the best media route.
  • By default WebRTC should be able to negotiate direct peer-to-peer connections when possible.
  • It should be possible to configure WebRTC not to disclose private local addresses. This is not required to be the default, because no defined mechanism satisfies that together with direct peer-to-peer connections.
  • By default WebRTC traffic should not go through proxy servers, but it should be possible to force it through a configured proxy.
sections.eli5: The rules try to keep calls working well while telling the website as little as possible, and let you choose a stricter setting if you want.

sections.title: The Four Modes and Their Defaults
sections.content:
The RFC defines four modes of behavior:

  • Mode 1, enumerate all addresses: WebRTC MUST use all network interfaces to contact STUN servers, TURN servers or peers. It finds the best media path but discloses the most.
  • Mode 2, default route plus associated local addresses: WebRTC MUST follow the kernel routing table, so media usually takes the same route as HTTP traffic. If an enterprise TURN server is present, the preferred route MUST be through it. The private IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of the chosen interface MUST be provided as host candidates, so direct connections still work.
  • Mode 3, default route only: As Mode 2, but the associated private addresses MUST NOT be provided. Traffic may hairpin through a NAT, fall back to an application TURN server, or fail altogether.
  • Mode 4, force proxy: As Mode 3, but when HTTP traffic goes through a proxy, media MUST be proxied too. If the proxy does not support UDP, UDP is disabled and TCP carries the media, with reduced quality.

Mode 1 MUST NOT be used unless user consent has been provided. The consent mechanism is left to the implementation, for example tying it to getUserMedia device permission consent described in RFC 8827. Without consent, Mode 2 SHOULD be used. Implementations MAY choose stricter modes, and future documents may define new modes or change the recommended defaults.

An organization can still force external WebRTC traffic through a proxy or enterprise TURN server using a firewall policy that only lets WebRTC leave that way, while intra-organization traffic stays direct.
sections.eli5: There are four settings, from telling the website everything to sending the whole call through a go-between. Without your permission, the browser uses the middle setting that shares only what is needed for a direct call.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
To follow normal routing as Modes 2 and 3 require, the simplest approach is to bind() the peer-to-peer sockets to the wildcard addresses (0.0.0.0 for IPv4, :: for IPv6). The OS then routes WebRTC traffic as it would HTTP traffic.

Mode 2 also needs the associated local address, defined as the source address that would be used for packets sent to the web application host. Using that host as the destination gives the right answer even for an intranet application. The steps are:

  1. Resolve the host in the web application URI to a remote IPv4 or IPv6 address. Behind a proxy that cannot be resolved via DNS, the proxy address can be used. For a file:// page, a well-known DNS name or IP address can be used.
  2. Create a UDP socket, bind() it to the wildcard address, and connect() it to that remote IP. This typically assigns a local address from the kernel routing table without sending packets.
  3. Query the socket with getsockname() or the equivalent to read the local address.
sections.eli5: To find out which of its own addresses it would use to reach a website, the browser quietly asks the computer which one it would pick, without actually sending anything.

sections.title: Guidance for Applications
sections.content:
The recommendations may cause some WebRTC applications to malfunction, so the RFC gives two guidelines for applications:

  • Applications SHOULD deploy a TURN server that supports both UDP and TCP connections to the server. Connectivity can then still be established when Mode 3 or 4 is in use, as long as the TURN server can be reached.
  • Applications SHOULD detect when they lack the full set of ICE candidates by checking for host candidates. If none are present, Mode 3 or 4 is in use, which is useful for diagnostics.
sections.eli5: If the browser is hiding addresses, a call may need a middleman server to work. Apps should have one ready and be able to notice when the browser is being private.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single statement: the document describes several potential privacy and security concerns with WebRTC peer-to-peer connections and gives mechanisms and recommendations for implementations to address them. The substance of the privacy analysis is in the problem statement and the modes.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about privacy, so the security section just points back to it. It asks nothing of the registry office.
